items.followUp: Differentiate between a dilute solution and a concentrated solution.

rubric.why: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a specified temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it contains the maximum amount of solute at a given temperature.

rubric.why: An unsaturated solution can still dissolve additional solute at that temperature.
rubric.description: Defines an unsaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it can dissolve more solute.

modelAnswer: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent at a particular temperature.
An unsaturated solution contains less than this maximum amount and can dissolve more solute at that temperature.

items.followUp: Why does a colloidal solution show the Tyndall effect while a true solution does not?

rubric.why: Particles in a true solution are too small to scatter light visibly.
rubric.description: Explains why true solutions do not show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the very small solute particles to the absence of visible light scattering.

rubric.why: Suspension particles are large and settle out, so they do not produce the visible Tyndall cone characteristic of colloids.
rubric.description: Explains why suspensions do not show the Tyndall effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the large, settling particles or their opaque nature.

modelAnswer: In a true solution, solute particles are too small to scatter light, so no visible Tyndall effect is observed.
Suspension particles are large and settle on standing (and may make the mixture opaque), so they do not produce the visible Tyndall cone characteristic of colloids.

items.followUp: Name two non-metals found in living organisms and state one role they play.

rubric.why: Several non-metals are essential constituents of living organisms.
rubric.description: Names essential non-metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming at least two relevant non-metals, such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen or nitrogen.

rubric.why: These elements form important biological compounds and are required for life.
rubric.description: Explains their importance to life.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking non-metals to the formation of biological compounds or to living matter.

modelAnswer: Non-metals such as carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen are essential constituents of living organisms.
They form important compounds of life, including proteins and carbohydrates.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of aluminium chloride using the criss-cross method.

rubric.why: The method depends on writing the symbols and valencies, then interchanging the valencies as subscripts.
rubric.description: States the formula-writing method.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for writing symbols and valencies, and 1 for interchanging valencies as subscripts and simplifying if possible.

rubric.why: Magnesium chloride demonstrates the method with valencies 2 and 1.
rubric.description: Gives a correct binary-compound example.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for a correct example with its formula; award 1 if the formula is correct but the valencies or method are not shown.

rubric.why: A second example shows correct use of the method, including a polyatomic ion where applicable.
rubric.description: Gives another correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second correct formula, such as aluminium oxide or calcium hydroxide.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the ions or elements and write their valencies above them.
Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts; reduce them to the simplest whole-number ratio, if possible.
For magnesium chloride: Mg has valency 2 and Cl has valency 1; therefore, the formula is MgCl₂.
For aluminium oxide: Al has valency 3 and O has valency 2; therefore, the formula is Al₂O₃.
For calcium hydroxide: Ca has valency 2 and OH has valency 1; therefore, the formula is Ca(OH)₂.

items.followUp: Explain the formation of the hydronium ion as an example of a coordinate covalent bond.

rubric.why: In a coordinate covalent bond, the shared electron pair is donated by one atom.
rubric.description: Defines a dative covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that the bond involves a shared pair of electrons and that both electrons are supplied by one atom.

rubric.why: The donor supplies a lone pair to an electron-deficient acceptor.
rubric.description: Identifies the donor and acceptor roles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that a donor atom supplies a lone pair to an acceptor.

rubric.why: Ammonium is formed when nitrogen in ammonia donates a lone pair to H⁺.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example, preferably ammonia forming the ammonium ion.

modelAnswer: A dative covalent bond is a covalent bond in which both electrons of the shared pair are donated by one atom.
The atom donating the lone pair is the donor; the atom accepting it is the acceptor.
For example, in NH₃, nitrogen donates a lone pair to H⁺ to form NH₄⁺.
This bond may be represented by an arrow from the donor to the acceptor: H₃N→H⁺.

items.followUp: Give five differences between Rutherford’s atomic model and Bohr’s atomic model.

rubric.why: Rutherford allowed electrons to move in any orbit, whereas Bohr proposed fixed energy levels or shells.
rubric.description: Compares electron orbits and energy levels.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for correctly contrasting unrestricted orbits with Bohr’s fixed energy levels.

rubric.why: Rutherford’s model could not explain atomic stability; Bohr’s model described stable orbits in which electrons do not radiate energy.
rubric.description: Compares the explanation of atomic stability.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for the contrast between Rutherford’s failure to explain stability and Bohr’s stable, non-radiating orbits.

rubric.why: Bohr explained that radiation is absorbed or emitted when electrons move between energy levels.
rubric.description: Compares how radiation is emitted or absorbed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr linked radiation to electron transitions between energy levels.

modelAnswer: 1. Rutherford proposed that electrons revolve around the nucleus in any orbit; Bohr proposed that electrons occupy only certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
2. Rutherford’s model did not assign fixed energies to electron orbits; Bohr’s model assigned a definite energy to each allowed orbit.
3. Rutherford’s model could not explain why revolving electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus; Bohr’s model explained atomic stability through stable orbits.
4. In Rutherford’s model, an accelerating electron should continuously radiate energy; in Bohr’s model, an electron in a permitted orbit does not radiate energy.
5. Rutherford’s model did not explain the line spectra of atoms; Bohr explained them by absorption or emission of energy when electrons jump between energy levels.

items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? Describe how crystals can be obtained from it by cooling.

rubric.why: A supersaturated solution holds more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature.
rubric.description: Defines a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for stating that it contains more solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature and noting that it is unstable, if included.

rubric.why: Heating allows more solute to dissolve and is used to prepare the starting saturated solution.
rubric.description: Describes the preparation of the hot saturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for preparing a saturated solution at a high temperature.

rubric.why: Careful cooling of the hot saturated solution can leave more solute dissolved than is normally possible at the lower temperature.
rubric.description: Describes cooling to obtain a supersaturated solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the hot saturated solution is cooled carefully, without disturbance, to form the supersaturated solution.

modelAnswer: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution can normally hold at the same temperature; it is unstable.
Prepare a saturated solution of the solute at a high temperature.
Cool the hot saturated solution slowly and carefully without disturbing it.
The cooled solution can retain excess dissolved solute and is then supersaturated.

items.followUp: State why air is a mixture and carbon dioxide is a compound.

rubric.why: The substances in a soft drink are mixed physically and their proportions may vary.
rubric.description: Explains why a soft drink is a mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning physical mixing or variable proportions of its components.

rubric.why: Water is a pure compound whose elements are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
rubric.description: Explains why water is a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

modelAnswer: A soft drink is a mixture because its ingredients are physically mixed and can be present in variable proportions.
Water is a compound because hydrogen and oxygen are chemically combined in a fixed ratio.
